newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine mkts focus on likely upgrade, not on Fed.
newsitem.headline: Argentine mkts focus on likely upgrade, not on Fed.

text.p: Argentina's markets are likely to brush off a hike in U.S. interest rates and instead remain focused on a widely expected upgrade in the country's credit rating, analysts said.
"The rising confidence in Argentina would offset the impact of one rate hike" in the U.S., said Frank McGann, vice-president at Merrill Lynch Argentina.

The U.S. Federal Reserve's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee meets Tuesday and there is speculation it will lift its target for the overnight Federal funds rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 5.50 percent.

But in Argentina attention is focused elsewhere. The most important engine of optimism in Argentina is the now general expectation that the country's credit rating will be upped by the international credit rating agencies shortly.
Two weeks ago, Standard & Poor's said it was reviewing the countries' BB-minus grade, adding that the outcome of the review will be complete within two or three weeks.
Argentina's Economy Minister Roque Fernandez commented recently: "On the basis of the information that we have, I can say that relatively quickly Argentina's credit rating will be upgraded."
One traditional fear in Argentina when the U.S. is about to tighten monetary policy is that it will slow the inflow of funds to the country as its higher yields become relatively less attractive.
Argentina's economy has been particularly sensitive to changes in U.S. monetary policy due to Convertibility, the system that pegs the peso to the dollar at par.

But Argentina's economy is currently in a much stronger position to stave off the impact of slightly higher costs of borrowing in dollars than it was before the Tequila crisis following the Mexican devaluation at the end of 1994.
"Our economy is more solid (than during the Tequila crisis), especially the financial system," said Jose Rutman, an economist at consultants Broda y Asociados.
Carlos Rodriguez, chief advisor to the Economy Ministry, told journalists Monday he did not expect investment in the country to be upset by a small rate hike in the U.S.
"Direct investment comes to Argentina under long-term investment programs with profits that will not be altered by a one percentage point change (in the U.S. long bond yield)," he said.

And, "a quarter or a half point hike will not detain the flow of capital to Argentina," said Sergio Galvan, head of research at Bansud. "This will be nothing like the scale of the rate hikes in 1994."
Galvan added that Argentine bonds could well rise to their highs of earlier this year on upgrade news.
"Good growth and falling country risk will be positive for the markets," said McGann.
The government estimates gross domestic product growth in excess of five percent this year after expansion of 4.6 percent in 1996.

"I do not think a lot will happen to stocks and bonds and there will be no changes to Argentina's financing policy, only that new debt will be slightly more expensive," said Jose Luis Espert, director of consultancy Econometrica.
"Nor will a hike in rates of the size that is being forecast hurt growth, since liquidity will remain high," he added.

The increased independence of the economy from U.S. monetary policy is in large part thanks to the introduction of the private pension fund system in mid-1994, which has boosted the domestic savings rate significantly.
At the end of last year, funds under management rose to $5.33 billion, up from $2.50 billion at the end of 1995.
((-- Buenos Aires Newsroom, 541 318-0668))
